module_title: Section 3(d), Compulsory Licensing, and Traditional Knowledge
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, UPSC Mains, and corporate litigators, this level explores the absolute frontiers of Indian IPR jurisprudence. It details India's unique battle against pharmaceutical 'Evergreening', the mechanics of Compulsory Licensing, and the protection of Indigenous Knowledge.

core_concepts.title: Section 3(d) of Patents Act: Anti-Evergreening
core_concepts.description:
India's most famous and debated patent law provision.
- The Issue: 'Evergreening' is a tactic where pharma companies make tiny, insignificant changes to an expiring patented drug to get a fresh 20-year patent, keeping prices artificially high.
- The Rule: Section 3(d) states that the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does **not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy** of that substance is NOT patentable.
- Landmark Case: *Novartis v. Union of India (2013)*. The Supreme Court rejected Novartis's patent for the cancer drug Glivec, holding that the new beta-crystalline form did not show significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy over the old version.

core_concepts.title: Compulsory Licensing (Section 84, Patents Act)
core_concepts.description:
A powerful tool to ensure public access to life-saving inventions.
- The Mechanism: After 3 years of a patent being granted, any person can apply to the Controller of Patents for a 'Compulsory License' to make the product without the owner's permission.
- The Triggers (Conditions): (1) The reasonable requirements of the public have not been satisfied, (2) The patented invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price, OR (3) The patented invention is not worked in the territory of India.
- Landmark Case: *Natco Pharma v. Bayer (2012)*. India granted its first compulsory license to Natco to manufacture a generic version of Bayer's highly expensive cancer drug Nexavar, slashing the price by 97%.

core_concepts.title: Traditional Knowledge (TK) and Biopiracy
core_concepts.description:
Biopiracy is the unauthorized appropriation of biological resources and traditional knowledge of indigenous communities (e.g., US companies trying to patent Neem's fungicidal properties or Turmeric's healing properties).
- Defense Mechanism: India created the **Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL)**. It translates ancient Ayurvedic, Unani, and Siddha texts into major international languages so foreign patent offices can instantly reject patent applications based on existing Indian traditional knowledge (destroying the 'Novelty' requirement).

core_concepts.title: Moral Rights in Copyright (Section 57)
core_concepts.description:
Also known as *Droit Moral*. Even if an author completely sells/assigns their copyright to a publisher, they retain two eternal 'Moral Rights':
1. Right of Paternity: The right to claim authorship of the work.
2. Right of Integrity: The right to restrain or claim damages for any distortion, mutilation, or modification of the work that would be prejudicial to the author's honor or reputation.

important_entities.name: Bolar Provision (Section 107A)
important_entities.significance: A brilliant pro-public health provision. It allows generic drug manufacturers to conduct research and development using a patented drug *while the patent is still active*, so they can apply for regulatory approvals and launch their cheap generic version the exact day the 20-year patent expires.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The 'Patent on Methods of Treatment' Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams often ask: 'Can a brilliant doctor patent a new, highly effective surgical method to cure heart disease?' **NO**. Under Section 3(i) of the Patents Act, any method of medical, surgical, curative, or diagnostic treatment of human beings or animals is expressly **not patentable** in India. You can patent the surgical *tool* (the scalpel), but not the *method*.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Needs not met, Price too high, Not made in India
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: These are the exact three statutory grounds under Section 84 that allow the government to break a patent monopoly.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains (GS 3 or Law Optional), when evaluating India's IPR regime, you MUST anchor your answer around the balance between protecting innovation and public health, citing **Section 3(d) (Novartis)** and **Section 84 (Natco v. Bayer)**.
